newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian election - profiles of contenders.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian election - profiles of contenders.

text.p: Bulgaria is voting on Sunday in a presidential election run-off between Petar Stoyanov, candidate of the united opposition, and the Socialist Ivan Marazov.
Following are profiles of the candidates:
PETAR STOYANOV, 44, vice-chairman of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), took 43.93 percent in Sunday's first round of voting.
A pro-market liberal, he favours closer ties with NATO and the European Union and criticises the Socialists for avoiding a clear position on the issue.
He made pre-election visits to Germany and Poland where he met Chancellor Helmut Kohl and President Aleksander Kwasniewski.

At an election night news conference last Sunday he said he expected to win the second round and one of his first acts would be to ask Prime Minister Zhan Videnov to reveal the full extent of Bulgaria's economic crisis.
"I will be pressing him to come forward with concrete solutions," he said.

A professional politician but untainted by the past, he offers a younger, slicker image and his speaking style is more pragmatic and businesslike than the philosophical speeches of outgoing president Zhelyu Zhelev.
Stoyanov defeated Zhelev in a U.S.-style primary election in June, winning 66 percent of votes cast, and is running as the candidate of the united opposition.
He has made a particular effort to appeal to young voters and has the support of Bulgaria's international soccer stars Hristo Stoichkov and Emil Kostadinov.

Stoyanov was born on May 25, 1952 in Plovdiv and studied law at Sofia University. He practised law in Plovdiv and became deputy justice minister in the first UDF government from 1991 to 1992, and was elected to parliament in December 1994.
A former volleyball player, he is married with two children. His wife is a diplomat at the Bulgarian embassy in London.
IVAN MARAZOV, 54, the culture minister and Bulgarian Socialist Party candidate, trailed a humiliating 17 points behind Stoyanov after the first round.
At an election night news conference, he blamed voter disillusionment with the government's handling of the economy for his defeat, and reformers in the party say a split is now inevitable.
A scholar of Thracian mythology, Marazov was drawn into politics on a joint ticket with Foreign Minister Georgy Pirinski, whose candidacy was rejected because he was born in the United States.
He models himself on other East European intellectuals who became heads of state after the fall of communism in 1989.

He prefers open-necked shirts and sweaters to the formal wear of party functionaries, but diligently attends party rallies commemorating dates in communist history and speaks nostalgically of the low prices in pre-1989 Bulgaria and lost Russian markets for Bulgaria's lacklustre industrial goods.

His "Together for Bulgaria" campaign has had the difficult task of appealing equally to the Socialists' two main constituencies -- private entrepreneurs and to older voters nostalgic for the security of the former one-party regime.
Born on March 15, 1942 in the village of Pirne near the Black Sea port of Bourgas, he trained as an art historian and edited a major Bulgarian art magazine during the communist regime.

Married with one child, Marazov entered politics as deputy culture minister in the first post-communist caretaker government in 1991. He headed the Art History Institute of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences between 1988 and 1992.
